<explanation>
This project is the GitHub Linguist repository – a Ruby library used on GitHub to detect file languages, ignore binaries or vendored files, suppress generated diffs, and generate language breakdown graphs. Given its purpose, a detailed system design diagram should capture both its high‐level Ruby library architecture and its integration points with native components and external dependencies.

1. Identify the main components:
   • Core Ruby Library: Represent the “lib/linguist” directory that contains the primary Ruby classes (e.g. linguist.rb, classifier.rb, heuristics.rb, repository.rb) which encapsulate the language detection algorithms.
   • Native Extensions: Include the “ext/linguist” folder where components in C (such as lexers and tokenizers) are built. These extend the core Ruby code for performance.
   • Command-Line Interface: Include the “bin/github-linguist” and “bin/git-linguist” scripts that provide CLI usage (and reference to the executable behavior described in the README).
   • Tools and Grammar Compiler: Depict the “tools/grammars” subdirectory which includes a standalone grammar compiler (with components written in Go and others) used to compile or manage language grammars.
   • Tests: Show the “test” directory that holds various tests (for blob, classifier, file blob, heuristics, repository, samples, etc.) to ensure the system behaves as expected.
   • Documentation and Samples: Represent the “docs”, “samples”, and “readme” that provide usage, guidelines, and example language files; these help users and contributors understand and extend Linguist.
   • External Dependencies: Illustrate integration with external libraries such as charlock_holmes (for character encoding) and rugged (for Git repository access), including their underlying native dependencies (like ICU, pkg-config, libcurl, OpenSSL, etc).

2. Determine interactions and relationships:
   • The Ruby entry-point (CLI) uses the core library classes to load a Git repository (via Rugged), process file blobs, and then classify languages using heuristic rules (contained in “lib/linguist/heuristics.rb” and “lib/linguist/classifier.rb”).
   • Native extension modules support the Ruby code when intensive processing (like tokenization or lexing) is required. Depict directional arrows from the Ruby core to the native modules.
   • The tools (in “tools/grammars”) can be represented as a separate component that both consumes and produces grammar data for the library. They might interact with the core via configuration files (grammar definitions, overrides, etc.).
   • The test suite runs against these components to confirm their integration; draw arrows from the test framework to both the core and native modules.
   • External libraries (rugged and charlock_holmes) are injected into the system at runtime, so represent them as dependency nodes interfacing with the core Ruby application.

3. Architectural patterns/design principles:
   • Modular Design: The project is clearly separated into core library code, native extensions, CLI tools, and testing – each in its own directory.
   • Dependency Injection & Extensibility: The README emphasizes how Linguist can be overridden and its behavior changed. This points out an extensible design where heuristics and language definitions are configurable.
   • Command Line as an Adapter: The CLI scripts act as adapters between a user’s command environment and the underlying programmatic API.

4. Relevant technologies to highlight:
   • Ruby and its gem ecosystem (as the main language)
   • Native C extensions (in “ext”)
   • External dependencies (ICU, zlib, libcurl, OpenSSL, etc.) which can be represented as peripheral services utilized by charlock_holmes and rugged.
   • Docker and Continuous Integration components in .devcontainer, Dockerfiles, and GitHub workflows that support development and testing.

5. Guidelines for tailoring the diagram:
   • Since Linguist is a library meant for language detection (often used as a backend service on GitHub), emphasize the separation between:
       - User interfaces (CLI, Docker interface)
       - Core language identification logic (the Ruby modules)
       - Performance-critical native routines (C extensions)
       - Integration with Git and file system access (using rugged)
   • Use appropriately shaped and colored boxes:
       - Blue boxes for Ruby modules,
       - Green boxes for native C extensions,
       - Orange boxes for CLI and tooling scripts,
       - Grey/transparent shapes for external dependencies.
   • Clearly label each component and show directional arrows illustrating data flow:
       - From “Repository” inputs (via Rugged) to the classification process in Linguist,
       - From the core library to native extension modules,
       - And from tests to their target components.

6. Final diagram elements to include:
   - A “User/CLI/Environment” block at the top that feeds input (files, Git revision) into the system.
   - A primary “Core Linguist Engine” block (divided into modules for blob processing, classification, heuristics, repository wrapping).
   - A “Native Extensions” block connected to the core engine.
   - A “Tools & Grammar Compiler” block that is linked to configuration and grammar data.
   - External “Dependencies” nodes (rugged, charlock_holmes, plus underlying packages like ICU, zlib, etc.).
   - A “Tests” block that covers all layers.
   - Optionally, blocks for “Continuous Integration” and “Containers” to indicate deployment and development support.

By breaking down the project into as many components as possible and capturing the dependencies and interactions, your system design diagram will provide a clear, detailed architectural overview tailored specifically for Linguist.
</explanation>
